thread.title: How To Retire Today Without Risking Grandma's Retirement

author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: How To Retire Today Without Risking Grandma's Retirement
text:
This research report was produced by The REIT Forum with assistance from Big Dog Investments .
The first rule of investing is to protect your principal. Many investors are so focused on the upside that they completely ignore the downside risks.
Every day, analysts are touting stocks for their upside. Few of the buy ratings include an adequate discussion of the risk factors. It is great that a stock might go up by 20% or 30%, but it could still be unappealing if the stock has a similar probability to fall by that amount.
This is even more important for retirees. When the investor is already retired, there is dramatically less new income available to correct investing mistakes. The investor should be focusing on protecting their portfolio rather than hunting for substantial gains. The worst problem in seeing investors swing for the fences is what happens when they have a couple of investments go south early on.
Investing in poor investments often leads to getting upset at something besides lack of due diligence. For instance, blaming these leaves:
Source: Imgur
Usually, investors blame management, but they might as well blame the leaves. Management should be a known risk.
The loss of principal often leads to a gambling mentality in an attempt to win back the losses. It leads investors to take on dramatically too much risk.
Source: Imgur
There is a better way to build the portfolio.
A better retirement Investors who want a more peaceful retirement should emphasize a more peaceful retirement account. Volatility should be scorned. Investors who are married to Modern Portfolio Theory may struggle with the lessons here.
Under Modern Portfolio Theory, the only return available is compensation for risk.
Under Modern Portfolio Theory, the investor can do nothing but diversify and reduce expenses.
Under this theory, investing in individual stocks is nothing more than gambling.
This is one area where Modern Portfolio Theory is wrong.
The problem with Modern Portfolio Theory is it relies on efficient markets. Efficient markets assumes that the markets are perfectly efficient at all times. Consequently, it would assume that a better-constructed ETF should have a higher expense ratio.
This is clearly not the case.
Higher expenses regularly lead to underperformance.
I want to focus on keeping expenses low and the portfolio quality high.
A higher quality portfolio There are a few ways investors can focus their efforts on higher quality stocks.
One of the simpler techniques is to utilize the credit rating agencies. The companies with higher credit ratings should generally be higher quality. That doesn’t mean that they will always outperform. It does mean that they will generally be better prepared for a difficult economic environment.
The credit rating agencies also won’t stop an investor from filling their portfolio with only stocks from 1 or 2 subsectors. A solid portfolio should include more diversity.
Real estate is the backbone of a strong portfolio When investors are building a diversified portfolio, they should still select their core areas. Real estate is an excellent addition to a portfolio. Surely most retirees would be comfortable if they owned an apartment building with minimal debt and had a trustworthy manager operating it for them at a very reasonable cost. It would be very reasonable to assume that the cash flows from that apartment building could cover their expenses year after year.
Ironically, many of these investors are still scared of buying REITs because interest rates may go up. I specifically said that they may go up rather than they will go up. If investors are dead certain that rates will continue to rise, they can use options contracts on treasury ETFs and make a fortune. Of course, they might be wrong even though they were certain.
They would still be gambling with their retirement. It is better to simply say that rates may go up.
Despite the potential for increasing rates, many investors would still be comfortable buying physical real estate. They might get some comfort out of using less debt leverage or having a long maturity on that leverage. If that’s the case, AvalonBay ( AVB ) and Equity Residential ( EQR ) should be near the top of their investment list. Both REITs have A- credit ratings with long weighted average maturities on their debt and low-interest rates.
Pick an area to excel in Many investors struggle with total returns over time. One of the major factors leading to underperformance is the tendency to buy high and sell low. The best method I’ve found to avoid that problem is building expertise within a few sectors.
Experts still make mistakes, but it is much easier to be comfortable with the share price if the investor is very familiar with the comparable stocks. They can isolate when one stock is deviating from their peers.
It is important to recognize whether that stock’s performance is being exaggerated relative to the sector or if the stock has fundamental flaws.
Let’s use a couple of examples:
In late 2017, I began purchasing Taubman Centers ( TCO ). Shares were about $50. Shares continued to decline and I continued to buy near the bottom around $45.
Source: Seeking Alpha
Many investors said I was simply wrong and betting on a terrible failing stock.
The green boxes are the times I purchased TCO. I continued to buy and be “wrong” as the stock plunged to $45. From that moment onwards, I was right. The stock rallied back to surpass $65 in a short period.
The purple box is when I closed out my entire position for a substantial gain. It took multiple sales throughout this period.
My confidence came from understanding the value of the real estate for each of the mall REITs. Since I also knew these valuations for Simon Property Group ( SPG ), General Growth Properties ( GGP ), and Macerich ( MAC ), I was quite comfortable initiating and expanding my position in TCO. This is the benefit of expertise within a sector.
Let’s move to the opposite side of the equation:
Another stock that was plunging last year was RAIT Financial ( RAS ). Some investors were confident that RAS would turn the situation around. They believed they were being paid handsomely to wait because of the high dividend yield. Many also cited the REIT’s book value as a reason to believe it was undervalued. Book value is a very important metric for a mortgage REIT. Investors should use the book value as one part of their analysis. When I dived into RAS, I found the book value was doing a poor job of telling the whole story. The expenses for RAS were completely out of control. I referred to the stock as a dead dividend walking.
Shares plunged from over $1 to $0.15 in the following months.
Source: Schwab
The dividend was cut to zero and there does not appear to be any compelling plan to keep the company afloat. As of my writing, shares are now under $0.09.
When investors grab a falling knife without the expertise in evaluating the underlying assets, they risk losing their fingers. Those investors lost the dividend yield and over 90% of their capital based on their unrealized loss.
Finding a safe dividend stock There are a few traits investors can look for in evaluating dividend safety. For an equity REIT, the coverage ratio from FFO is one useful metric. However, there are often non-recurring gains or losses included in FFO. Management of some REITs will provide useful adjustments to normalize the value from one period to another. Management of less desirable REITs will provide adjustments that completely fail to represent the underlying performance of the company. As you might imagine, their adjustments will be designed to make their company look better.
There are three ways to get past poor quality accounting:
The first method is to spend a few years learning REIT accounting and which adjustments should be stripped out. The other is to find someone you can rely on to check those numbers.
The second method is to look at the company’s size. Yes, it is that simple. Larger companies have more analysts, like me, following them. They are more likely to be called out for poor quality accounting. Most of the terrible adjustments I’ve witnessed come from companies with a market capitalization of under $2 billion. This method is less reliable than the first one.
The third method is to check the amount of stock-based compensation. Some REITs attempt to remove stock-based compensation in their adjustments for non-recurring charges. This is usually a recurring charge and removing it is a poor quality adjustment. It should set off red flags for the investor.
Other traits of solid dividend stocks Investors can avoid accounting or business plans that are needlessly complex. Investors have an easy time understanding triple net lease REITs. The three best triple net lease REITs are Realty Income ( O ), National Retail Properties ( NNN ), and STORE Capital ( STOR ). These REITs all strive for transparency in their business model and accounting. Their presentations are designed to educate investors about the metrics they demonstrate their stability over a long period. STOR has a short track record compared to NNN and O but is otherwise comparable.
While these 3 REITs have clear business plans and solid accounting, that doesn’t make the valuations attractive. I’ve found several other REITs I believe offer superior alternatives at this time.
Simple REITs There are plenty of other simple businesses to understand. The apartment REIT is about as simple as apartment buildings. They simply own far more buildings and currently many of them are priced at a dramatic discount to the fair value of the buildings they own. The apartments are rented out to tenants and create a steady stream of revenue. Leases are generally 1 year or less so the REIT can adjust pricing quickly if we see higher inflation.
The other 5 big apartment REITs ( after AVB and EQR ) are Essex Property Trust ( ESS ), Apartment Investment & Management Company ( AIV ), UDR, Inc. ( UDR ), Camden Property Trust ( CPT ), and Mid-America Apartment Communities ( MAA ). These apartment REITs all have conservative balance sheets and excellent operating fundamentals. Some of them are valued more attractive than others, but none of the big 7 would be a terrible choice.
Other easy businesses Outside of REITs, there are still plenty of easy businesses to understand. Altria Group ( MO ) and Philip Morris ( PM ) sell tobacco products. Their number 1 expense is sin taxes. Their margins are excellent even after the taxes. Their earnings have been steady and climbing. They use most of their earnings to pay a substantial dividend yield. The share price has plunged for each of them since June 2017. The decline has been a combination of rising yields giving investors alternatives for reliable income and analysts failing to model growth effectively.
The failure of analysts to produce accurate long-term growth models appears to be the strongest factor in play. They were absurdly bullish back in June 2017 and encouraged investors to buy in at prices that were simply much too high. Today, they have given up on the stocks and investors are getting a much better opportunity.
There are a handful of other stocks that are also favored by many retirees, such as Visa ( V ), 3M ( MMM ), Apple ( AAPL ), Coca-Cola ( KO ), PepsiCo ( PEP ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Target ( TGT ), Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ), Verizon ( VZ ), and AT&T ( T ). However, investors may be seeking a higher overall yield.
Pumping up the dividend yield One area that many investors struggle with is finding a sufficient dividend yield. This challenge can lead them to speculate on stocks that are too risky rather than focusing on the kind of safer stocks I’ve mentioned here. When investors need to boost the yield on their portfolio, I believe one of the best techniques is using preferred shares. I put together an entire guide: see my guide to preferred shares . I also have a guide for preferred share dividend captures .
Allow me to share some insights on preferred shares:
Like common stocks, preferred shares rise and fall in price. One goal of diligent research is to find the best entry point. Even if you choose to hold your shares for a long period, you want to purchase them at the lowest price. The lowest price gets you the maximum shares for your investment and nets you the greatest dividend over time.
If you are a trader, you want to purchase your preferred shares at a discount and sell them at a premium, just as you would a common stock.
Preferred shares can be called by the issuing company at a fixed price (the call price) at any time after call protection ends. Usually, the call price is $25.00.
Because preferred shares have a built-in call value of $25, there is a strong tendency for the stock price to oscillate around $25.
For various reasons, such as a low dividend, some preferred shares trade at a discount most of the time. Others, with a high dividend, may trade at a premium to their call price.
Stop gambling Retirees need to focus on having a stable portfolio and a stable source of income.
Gambling for high upside may seem appealing, but the consequences are disastrous. Instead, investors can focus on finding stronger stocks with modestly lower yields. To compensate for the lower average yield on the common stocks, investors can supplement their portfolio with several preferred shares.
AVB and EQR are both in the buy range along with TCO. RAS remains a sell because I believe they are headed toward bankruptcy.
